title: The Anti-Semitism Playbook Comes for Indian Americans
text:
Updated at 5:48 p.m. ET on November 19, 2026 

 The far right has a habit of saying horrible, bigoted things about, well, almost everyone. But throughout the second Trump administration, it has taken a particularly keen interest in Indian Americans. Laura Loomer, the extremist provocateur, has called Indians “third world invaders” who are “shitting in the water they bathe and drink.” Jack Posobiec, a MAGA influencer, has declared that Indians are “scam migrants” who are part of a “mass immigration cartel.” Even some Rep ublican politicians and administration officials have joined in. Last year, a top DOGE staffer was unmasked as the man behind an anonymous X account that had posted, “Normalize Indian hate.” He resigned, then was quickly rehired for another government job.

 Many of the attacks against Indian Americans pull from a different script than the usual far-right anti-immigrant talking points. “Indians in America—they have very high educational attainment. They do economically very well,” Blake Neff, a co-host of The Charlie Kirk Show , recently said on the podcast. “We basically decided to replace our upper crust with people from a different cultural background, a totally different value system.” Instead of portraying Indian Americans as unauthorized border-crossers, welfare-state moochers, or unassimilated foreigners who can’t speak English, people like Neff paint them as a minuscule but high-achieving minority group that is using its power to covertly change the country.  

 [ Read: The mainstreaming of anti-Indian bigotry ] 

 Maybe this sounds familiar. A small, power-hungry cabal working to dominate America—the same trope that has long been used against Jewish people. “It’s the same kinds of ideas that we see in The Protocols of the Elders of Zion ,” the infamous anti-Semitic text first published more than a century ago, Pamela Nadell, a historian of American anti-Semitism at American University, told me. In the swell of anti-Indian hate, the anti-Semitic playbook is getting recycled and retooled to target a new swath of the country.

 Anti-Semitic conspiracy theories have long cast Jewish influence as a one-size-fits-all explanation for any event or grievance. Jews have been blamed for the bubonic plague, Abraham Lincoln’s assassination, and natural disasters supposedly set off by space lasers . Indian Americans are not (yet) a scapegoat on that scale, but they are acquiring the raw material that anti-Semitic conspiracy theories feed on: visibility and success. In sheer economic terms, Indians are the country’s richest minority group by a substantial margin. Indian American CEOs run Google, Microsoft, YouTube, Adobe, Perplexity, and IBM. With Kamala Harris and Usha Vance, the vice president’s residence has had back-to-back inhabitants who are of Indian descent. And the country’s two biggest cities, New York and Los Angeles, will be run by Indian American mayors come December.

 In the nativist view, Indians are succeeding not because of their hard work and embrace of American values, but because they are cheating and manipulating their way to the top. Indian Americans of all stripes have been targets of the far right’s attacks, even those tied to MAGA. (“What is this hatred? I don’t recognize it,” the former top Trump official Harmeet Dhillon wrote on X earlier this month after she was subjected to vicious online abuse.) Attacks on Indian Americans tap into nativist anxieties that the best jobs are going to them , not us . They have become avatars of a feeling that modern America is changing in unfamiliar ways. Just as conspiracists have long alleged that Jews exercise sinister control over Hollywood, they now also claim that Indians exert untoward influence over Silicon Valley.

 Some leading bigots are now blending these two hatreds, depicting Indians and Jews as one all-powerful evil force. Nick Fuentes, the young livestreamer who has expressed admiration for Adolf Hitler and denied the Holocaust, has said that Indians and Jews are “working together to rape your life.” He’s blamed both groups even for mundane problems such as annoying YouTube ads. “Indians will just milk every dollar out of you,” he said. “They do it at Google.” The conspiracist Stew Peters has likened Indians to “cockroaches” and “parasites” who are hogging high-paying tech jobs while also alleging that they have been imported into the United States as “Jewish bioweapons” to destroy Christian civilization. In an email, Peters doubled down on his comments. “The notion that critiquing the deliberate demographic replacement of White Americans by Jewish elites through mass Indian immigration constitutes anti-Semitic tropes is intellectually dishonest,” he told me. Jewish groups, Peters claimed, are “leveraging their disproportionate influence over media and finance to pathologize any resistance to this agenda as ‘racism’ or ‘anti-Semitism.’”

 [ Read: America’s next top racist ] 

 More often, prejudice against Indians—like anti-Semitism—operates with a veneer of plausible deniability. Nowhere is this more prominent than in discussions of H-1B visas, the program that companies, especially in Silicon Valley, use to hire high-skilled workers. There are f air and legitimate critiques of the program, but some opponents on the right treat H-1Bs less as a policy question and more as a pretense to make sweeping claims about Indians. Benny Johnson, an influencer who is a frequent presence at the White House , has said that Indian immigrants on H-1Bs are on a mission to “effectively colonize the West for the good of India.” Why did Texas go blue in the midterms? Blame the H-1Bs, Gregory Bovino, the former Border Patrol commander, posted on X . (One problem: H-1B visa holders can’t vote.)

 When I showed this rhetoric against Indian Americans to several experts on anti-Semitism, they immediately recognized the similarities. “Anti-Semitism is a seed bed of sorts,” James Loeffler, a professor of modern Jewish history at Johns Hopkins University, told me. “It creates a reservoir of stereotypes that then people dip into and project onto other groups.” Whether applied to Jews or Indians, such bigotry has the same end goal: to protect a white, Christian majority. To stop demographic change, nativists can’t just push for more mass deportations and closing up the border. Relatively few Indian Americans are undocumented, though that hasn’t stopped posts on X advocating for DEI: “deport every Indian.” By fixating on Indian Americans, the far right is attempting to find the ideas and rhetoric to convince the country that even the most successful immigrants are bad.

 Some on the right likely don’t realize they are grafting anti-Jewish tropes onto Indian Americans. (Nick Fuentes, Benny Johnson, Blake Neff, and Jack Posobiec did not respond to requests for comment.) Anti-Semitism is deeply entrenched in American life—especially on the right, where dog whistles about George Soros and “the globalists” run rampant. And as with anti-Semitism, hatred toward Indian Americans has real consequences. Last month, a crew of far-right activists stormed a Diwali celebration in Seattle and held up signs that read Deport all dot heads and Stop Hindu Replacement of Christians . A few weeks earlier, a 19-year-old Taco Bell cashier in Illinois told his co-worker that he “couldn’t wait to kill Indian people.” He allegedly drove to a Hindu temple outside of Chicago with an automatic rifle and hundreds of rounds of ammunition. Fortunately, his gun jammed. When the FBI later searched his apartment, they found a neo-Nazi patch and a gas canister inscribed with anti-Indian slurs. (According to the Associated Press , the man intends to plead not guilty to charges of terrorism.)

 Even something as innocuous as shopping at Costco can turn Indian Americans into targets of hate. You will find lots of aggrieved social-media posts about South Asians stocking up on Kirkland Signature–brand paper towels and $5 rotisserie chicken. “Why is the return line always FILLED w/Indians,” the MAGA political consultant Seth Weathers recently posted on X. In June, Sara Gonzales, a host on BlazeTV, went on a YouTube rant about how some Costcos now sell mangoes directly imported from India: “It makes sense, seeing as anytime I step into my local Costco, I feel like I’m in Mumbai.”

 I’ve watched with a mix of horror and dread as people who look like me have become targets. Are my parents safe in the Ohio suburbs? Perhaps this is just a fleeting moment of heightened animus. I hope so. Many Republican leaders are pushing back against the Indian bigotry within their own ranks. In September, Karl Rove said at The Atlantic Festival that he would vote for a Democrat for just the second time in his life to boycott Bo French, the GOP candidate for Texas railroad commissioner who posted about “the problem” of South Asian college-football fans. (French was trounced by his Democratic opponent earlier this month.)

 But everyone always wants someone to blame. Especially at a time of rampant fear that AI will wipe out the workforce, Indian Americans are an easy scapegoat. In the half century since America opened the door to Indian immigrants, they have quietly experienced something like a golden age in the U.S. Sundar Pichai was born in a house in Chennai that had no running water; now he reportedly lives in a mansion with an infinity pool. Kash Patel opened his Senate confirmation hearing for FBI director by greeting his parents in the audience with “Jai Shri Krishna.” Now Indians are learning a familiar truth. Minorities can do well in America. But prosperity is not the same as acceptance.
